messages.content: I want to design runtime verification for multicore embedded controllers. The design needs to preserve deadline guarantees and produce sound verdicts even though telemetry is asynchronous and may be lost.

That sets two constraints on the design: what the monitor may conclude from the telemetry it receives, and what running the monitor may cost the control jobs. Asynchronous telemetry can arrive later than the activity it describes, while lossy telemetry may leave gaps. The verification logic must account for those limits without compromising the controllers’ specified deadlines.
Can you state the verdict requirement precisely? I want verdicts to remain sound under telemetry loss.

A definitive verdict must be justified by the available evidence even when telemetry is missing. In particular, a gap in telemetry must not be treated as proof that an event did not occur. If the available observations leave a property undecidable, the monitor should not present a definitive conclusion that depends on filling that gap one way or the other. This is a soundness requirement; it does not require every case to receive a definitive verdict when telemetry is lost.
Does that mean loss prevents every useful verdict?

No. Soundness under loss does not say that every telemetry gap makes every conclusion impossible. It says that a verdict must not assert more than the evidence warrants. Whether a particular conclusion remains justified depends on what the property requires and what the received telemetry establishes. The requirement leaves the design of that reasoning open.
There is also a completeness condition, but it is narrower: bounded-response violations must be detected when telemetry is lossless.

Right. Under lossless telemetry, the monitor must not miss a bounded-response violation. A bounded-response condition concerns whether a required response occurs within its specified bound; a violation is a case where that condition is not met. The completeness guarantee applies to those violations in the lossless case. It does not, by itself, promise completeness for every kind of property or for traces with missing telemetry.
How do those two requirements fit together without contradicting each other?

They apply under different observation conditions. Soundness constrains definitive verdicts even if telemetry is lost. Completeness requires detection of bounded-response violations when telemetry is lossless. Thus the design cannot use uncertainty caused by loss to justify an unsupported verdict, yet it also cannot overlook a bounded-response violation merely because the telemetry is asynchronous when no telemetry has been lost.
So asynchronous delivery and telemetry loss are separate concerns?

Yes. Asynchrony concerns when observations become available relative to the activity being monitored; loss concerns whether observations are available at all. A late observation is not necessarily a missing one. The design must respect that distinction when drawing verdicts, but the goal does not prescribe a particular way to represent delays or gaps.
I do not want a late message, on its own, to be mistaken for evidence that a bounded response never happened.

That follows from the soundness requirement. If the conclusion depends on the absence of a response, uncertainty about the relevant telemetry cannot simply be converted into proof of absence. At the same time, with lossless telemetry, asynchronous arrival cannot become an excuse for failing to identify an actual bounded-response violation. Those are requirements on the resulting verdicts, not a specified implementation method.
Now for the runtime cost: monitoring may add no more than 5% worst-case execution time per control job, and all specified deadlines must still hold.

The overhead limit is per control job: monitoring adds ≤5% worst-case execution time to each control job. It is not merely an average overhead across jobs. Deadline preservation is a separate condition: staying within that 5% limit is not sufficient if any specified deadline is lost.
Why keep the percentage and the deadline condition separate?

They answer different questions. The ≤5% condition bounds the monitoring contribution to each control job’s worst-case execution time. The deadline condition asks whether the specified timing obligations still hold with monitoring present. The goal requires both, rather than treating the percentage as a substitute for deadline guarantees.
Does the goal give a particular deadline value or a telemetry delay bound?

No. It refers to all specified deadlines without listing their values, and it characterizes telemetry as asynchronous and lossy without supplying a delivery-delay bound. Those quantities should not be invented when stating the goal. The explicit numerical limit here is the monitoring overhead of ≤5% worst-case execution time per control job.
Would it be accurate to summarize the verdict target as ‘always detect bounded-response violations’?

That would omit an essential condition. The stated completeness target is detection of bounded-response violations when telemetry is lossless. Under telemetry loss, the stated requirement is sound verdicts, not unconditional detection of every such violation. Keeping that qualification matters because missing observations may limit what can be concluded.
And ‘sound’ should apply to the verdicts, not mean that the telemetry itself is reliable?

Exactly. The telemetry may be lost, and its asynchronous delivery is part of the setting. Soundness describes the monitor’s conclusions in that setting: a definitive verdict should not claim something the available evidence cannot support. It is not a claim that telemetry is complete under loss.
Please put the whole design goal in one formulation without choosing an implementation.

Design runtime verification for multicore embedded controllers that preserves deadline guarantees while producing sound verdicts despite asynchronous, lossy telemetry. Verdicts must remain sound under telemetry loss, and bounded-response violations must be detected when telemetry is lossless. Monitoring must add no more than 5% worst-case execution time per control job, while preserving all specified deadlines.

For the multicore runtime-verification design, I propose sequence-numbered per-core rings and completeness-watermarked, skew-aware three-valued monitors. I would budget instrumentation below 5% and verify the deadlines by response-time analysis.

That is a coherent proposal for addressing both sides of the goal. The per-core rings and sequence numbers organize the telemetry and make missing observations visible as uncertainty rather than silently treating them as nonexistent events. Completeness watermarks and skew-aware interpretation would govern when a monitor has enough information to decide a time-bounded property. Three-valued verdicts give it a way to say that the evidence is still inconclusive. Separately, the instrumentation budget addresses the per-job execution-time limit, while response-time analysis addresses preservation of the specified deadlines. These are proposed mechanisms and checks, not yet established guarantees.
What work does the sequence numbering do if each core already has its own ring?

A per-core ring identifies the source of a stream of observations; sequence numbering gives the monitor a way to reason about continuity within that stream. If the received sequence is incomplete, the monitor can recognize a possible telemetry gap rather than assuming that the observed entries tell the whole story. Sequence numbers alone do not reveal the contents of a missing entry, establish ordering between cores, or make a verdict sound. They provide information the monitor must interpret conservatively.
So I should not describe a gap as proof that a response failed to happen?

Correct. A gap says that relevant telemetry may be unavailable; it does not say what an unobserved event was. For a bounded-response condition, a monitor must not infer a violation merely because no response appears among observations known to be incomplete. The proposed three-valued interpretation can retain an inconclusive verdict where that uncertainty matters.
What exactly is meant by a completeness watermark here?

Conceptually, it marks how far the monitor can treat the relevant telemetry as complete for purposes of a decision. That is different from simply noting how recently an entry arrived: asynchronous delivery means that arrival order need not establish that all earlier relevant observations have been accounted for. The proposal names completeness watermarks but does not specify how they are computed or how far they advance under loss. Their role is to prevent a time-bounded conclusion from relying on an unsupported assumption of completeness.
How does skew awareness fit with the watermark? I do not want to conflate the two.

They address different uncertainties. Completeness concerns whether the observations needed for a conclusion have been accounted for. Skew awareness concerns how timing information from different cores may be interpreted when evaluating a temporal condition. A completeness watermark alone need not resolve cross-core timing uncertainty, and accounting for skew alone does not fill a telemetry gap. The monitor needs to respect both before issuing a definitive verdict that depends on them.
Is the third verdict value simply ‘unknown’?

Yes, ‘unknown’ or ‘inconclusive’ expresses the third value in this proposal. The other two values are definitive satisfaction and violation when warranted by the evidence. The point of three-valued monitoring is not to make missing telemetry harmless; it is to represent explicitly when missing or not-yet-complete information prevents a sound two-valued conclusion.
Would asynchronous delivery always force an unknown verdict?

No. Asynchrony may delay when a decision is justified, but it does not imply that a definitive verdict can never be reached. A completeness-watermarked, skew-aware monitor is intended to distinguish ‘not enough information yet’ from ‘enough information to decide.’ The proposal does not state a fixed delivery delay or a universal point at which every verdict becomes definitive.
How should I connect that to completeness for bounded-response violations when telemetry is lossless?

The design needs to ensure that, when telemetry is lossless, a genuine bounded-response violation is not left undetected. In that setting, the watermark and skew-aware reasoning must permit a justified violation verdict once the observations needed to establish it are available. Under telemetry loss, the requirement remains soundness of whatever verdict is issued; the proposal should not imply that every violation can still be detected despite missing observations.
If a monitor remains inconclusive while waiting for telemetry, is that itself a violation verdict?

No. Inconclusive means that the monitor has not justified either definitive verdict. For a bounded-response violation, the lossless-completeness requirement concerns eventual detection of an actual violation under lossless telemetry, not labeling a period of uncertainty as a violation. The proposal must keep that distinction clear.
On the timing side, why say ‘budget instrumentation below 5%’ when the requirement permits ≤5%?

They are different statements. The requirement permits monitoring to add no more than 5% worst-case execution time per control job. Budgeting instrumentation below 5% is the proposed design approach to that limit; it is not a claim that a measured or analyzed overhead already meets it. The specified threshold remains ≤5% per control job.
And response-time analysis is meant to establish the deadline part rather than infer it from that budget?

Exactly. Even if monitoring fits its per-job worst-case execution-time limit, that alone does not demonstrate that all specified deadlines remain satisfied. The proposal calls for response-time analysis to check deadline preservation with the monitoring costs included. It does not supply the analysis inputs or announce a result.
Can I present the rings and monitors as the verification design, with response-time analysis as a separate check on its timing impact?

Yes, as a proposed structure. Sequence-numbered per-core rings supply organized telemetry; completeness-watermarked, skew-aware three-valued monitors use it to produce verdicts without disguising relevant uncertainty. Instrumentation is to be budgeted below 5% worst-case execution time per control job, and response-time analysis is to verify that all specified deadlines are preserved. The verdict and timing properties still need to be established for the resulting design; this proposal does not itself report that they have been established.
How can completeness watermarks advance past dropped sequence numbers without turning unknown bounded-response outcomes into false violations?

They can advance past a known gap only if advancement does not mean ‘everything before this point was observed.’ The monitor needs to keep the gap visible as uncertainty. It may be able to say that it has finished accounting for what telemetry is available up to a point, but it must not infer from that progress that an unobserved response did not occur.
Isn’t a completeness watermark supposed to certify completeness? Advancing one across a gap sounds contradictory.

It would be contradictory if a single watermark certified that every relevant event before it had been observed. With a dropped sequence number, that claim is not justified merely because later entries have arrived. One way to frame the requirement is to distinguish progress through the stream from completeness of the evidence needed for a particular verdict. A watermark used to justify a violation cannot erase a gap that might contain the required response.
Suppose the monitor sees a request and then no response before the response bound. What changes if there was a dropped entry in between?

The dropped entry might have described the response. If so, the visible absence of a response is not proof that the response was absent. Even once the relevant time window has passed, the monitor cannot issue a violation verdict on that basis alone. For that request, the outcome remains inconclusive unless other available evidence is sufficient to settle it.
So reaching the end of the bounded-response window and having complete evidence are different things?

Yes. Reaching the end of the window addresses whether there is still time for the response to occur. Complete evidence addresses whether the monitor can tell what occurred within that window. To conclude that a required response failed to occur, both questions matter. A missing observation can leave the second question unresolved after the window has ended.
Could a watermark still move forward for other checks while that request remains unknown?

Conceptually, yes, provided the movement is not treated as a blanket certificate for every bounded-response outcome. A gap may matter to some conclusions and not to others. The essential rule is that any conclusion affected by the gap must retain its uncertainty; advancing a position in the telemetry stream must not silently convert that uncertainty into a violation.
How would I tell whether the dropped telemetry matters to a particular bounded-response check?

Ask whether an event consistent with the missing telemetry could change that check’s verdict. If a missing observation could have been the required response within the relevant bound, declaring a violation would be unsound. The proposal does not yet specify a particular procedure for deciding relevance, so that question needs to be handled explicitly rather than assumed away.
Does a sequence-number gap itself tell the monitor what kind of event was lost?

No. It indicates missing telemetry in that per-core sequence, not the contents of the missing entry. The monitor must not interpret the gap as either ‘a response occurred’ or ‘no response occurred’ without other grounds. That is why the inconclusive value is important.
What if entries after the gap have arrived? Can their arrival close the earlier uncertainty?

Their arrival can establish that the stream has continued, but it does not by itself recover what was dropped. Later observations might supply evidence that settles a particular verdict, depending on the property and their content. Merely passing the missing sequence number, however, cannot make an absence claim sound.
I’m trying to distinguish a delayed entry from a dropped entry. Does that affect when the monitor can decide?

It does. With asynchronous delivery, an entry may simply not have arrived yet; with a known gap, an entry may never be available. A monitor should not treat either situation as proof of absence while it could affect the verdict. The difference matters for whether uncertainty may later be resolved, but neither condition alone licenses a false violation.
Where does skew awareness enter this specific question?

A response may be observed yet still have uncertain placement relative to a bounded-response deadline when timing information comes from different cores. Skew awareness prevents the monitor from treating an uncertain temporal relationship as a settled one. It is distinct from the sequence gap: accounting for timing skew cannot reconstruct a lost entry, and recognizing a lost entry does not resolve cross-core timing uncertainty.
Would it be safe to say the watermark has advanced, but the verdict for an affected request is still unknown?

Yes, if ‘advanced’ is understood as progress that preserves the record of the gap, not as a claim that the affected request’s response window was fully observed. The verdict remains unknown where a missing event could change it. A definitive violation requires evidence that excludes a timely required response, not just a position beyond the response bound.
Does preserving unknown outcomes undermine the requirement to detect bounded-response violations?

Not in the stated form of that requirement. Completeness for bounded-response violations is required when telemetry is lossless. When telemetry is lost, the requirement is that verdicts remain sound. Retaining an unknown outcome rather than asserting an unsupported violation respects that distinction. In the lossless case, the monitor still needs to reach a violation verdict for an actual bounded-response violation.
Then the key issue is what the watermark is allowed to certify, rather than whether its position can move at all?

Exactly. A moving watermark cannot be used to claim complete knowledge across a dropped sequence number if that missing observation could affect the verdict. The monitor may track progress past the gap, but it must carry forward the associated uncertainty for affected bounded-response checks. Otherwise an unknown outcome could be mistaken for a violation solely because the watermark moved.
Here is a hypothesis for the watermark question: under ≤200-µs clock skew, gap-tainted windows stay unknown, while lossless watermarks detect every bounded-response violation after expiry.

That states a conditional behavior rather than an established result. With clock skew no greater than 200 µs, a window tainted by a telemetry gap retains an unknown verdict; advancing a watermark must not turn that gap into evidence of a violation. In the lossless case, the hypothesis says the watermarks enable detection of every bounded-response violation after the relevant response window expires.
What does ‘gap-tainted window’ mean in that statement?

It means a bounded-response window affected by missing telemetry. The missing observation could matter to what the monitor concludes about that window, so the hypothesis keeps its outcome unknown. The phrase does not say what the dropped observation contained.
Even if the watermark has moved beyond the window?

Yes. Under the hypothesis, watermark progress does not remove the uncertainty associated with a gap-tainted window. Moving beyond the window must not be interpreted as proof that no required response occurred in missing telemetry; its verdict stays unknown.
Does ‘unknown’ mean the monitor has found a violation but is withholding the announcement?

No. Unknown is not a violation verdict. It means the available telemetry does not justify resolving that gap-tainted window as either satisfied or violated under the stated hypothesis. Calling it a violation would lose the distinction the hypothesis is meant to preserve.
How does the ≤200-µs clock-skew condition affect the claim?

It is the stated condition under which the hypothesis is made. The value is inclusive: clock skew of 200 µs is within ≤200 µs. The hypothesis does not state what happens if skew exceeds that bound, and it does not provide a separate timing margin to add to any response bound.
Should I read 200 µs as the bounded-response deadline?

No. The 200-µs figure bounds clock skew in this hypothesis; it is not the response bound. ‘After expiry’ refers to expiry of the applicable bounded-response window, whose duration is not specified here.
Why say detection happens after expiry rather than as soon as a request is observed?

Before the response window expires, the required response may still occur within the bound. For a violation based on failure to respond in time, expiry matters because it marks the end of that opportunity. The hypothesis links detection of every bounded-response violation, in the lossless case, to that post-expiry condition; it does not claim a violation can be established simply upon observing a request.
Does ‘after expiry’ promise an immediate verdict at the exact expiry instant?

It does not specify an exact verdict latency or say that the verdict appears at the expiry instant. It says that, with lossless telemetry and under the stated skew condition, every bounded-response violation is detected after expiry. The hypothesis should not be embellished with a numerical delay that it does not give.
So the two parts cover different observation conditions?

Yes. Gap-tainted windows remain unknown when missing telemetry affects them. Lossless watermarks, by contrast, are hypothesized to detect every bounded-response violation after expiry. The first part protects against unsupported violation verdicts in the presence of gaps; the second states the desired detection behavior when telemetry is lossless. Both are stated under the ≤200-µs clock-skew condition.
If a sequence gap is visible but the window has expired, can I call that a detected bounded-response violation?

Not under this hypothesis if the window is gap-tainted. Expiry tells you the response period has ended, but the gap leaves the outcome unknown. The lossless-watermark claim applies when telemetry is lossless; it cannot be used to turn a gap-tainted window into a violation verdict.
Does the hypothesis say all outcomes in the lossless case are violations?

No. It concerns detecting every bounded-response violation when telemetry is lossless. It does not say that every bounded-response window is violated, nor does it specify a complete set of verdict rules for nonviolating windows.
What would we need to be careful about when phrasing the hypothesis as a claim about watermarks?

Keep the watermark’s role tied to the stated conditions. In a gap-tainted window, advancing it must leave the verdict unknown rather than implying complete knowledge of the missing telemetry. With lossless telemetry, the hypothesis is that watermarks support detection of every bounded-response violation after expiry. Neither clause, by itself, establishes that a particular monitor has been proved or tested to behave this way.
Can you restate it without implying the hypothesis has already been verified?

The hypothesis is that, under clock skew of ≤200 µs, gap-tainted bounded-response windows remain unknown despite watermark progress, while lossless watermarks detect every bounded-response violation after the relevant window expires. It is a proposed property to establish, not a reported verification result.
To evaluate the watermark hypothesis, I want to replay 10,000 gap-injected and lossless traces at ±200-µs skew, then check gap taint and violation completeness against an oracle.

That activity targets both parts of the hypothesis. The gap-injected traces let you check whether gap-tainted bounded-response windows stay unknown. The lossless traces let you check whether bounded-response violations identified by the oracle are detected after expiry. The proposed replay uses 10,000 traces across the gap-injected and lossless cases at ±200-µs skew; it does not yet report any results.
What does checking gap taint against the oracle mean here?

It means comparing the monitor’s treatment of windows affected by missing telemetry with the reference used for the check. For a gap-tainted window, the behavior under examination is whether the monitor retains an unknown outcome rather than turning the gap into a violation verdict. The activity names an oracle as the comparison reference but does not specify how that oracle is constructed.
And what is the lossless comparison looking for?

For the lossless traces, it looks for bounded-response violations in the oracle reference and checks whether the replayed monitor detects them after the applicable response window expires. That is the violation-completeness check. It should not be described as a check that every window is a violation.
Is the 10,000 count for each kind of trace?

The activity says to replay 10,000 gap-injected and lossless traces. It does not specify a count for each kind or a split between them, so I would describe 10,000 as the stated trace count without assigning a distribution.
I also want to be exact about ±200-µs skew. Is that the response bound?

No. ±200 µs is the skew setting for the replay. It is not the bounded-response duration, which is not given here. The check for violation completeness is tied to expiry of the applicable response window, not to the clock-skew value itself.
Does replaying at ±200 µs establish the hypothesis for every skew within ≤200 µs?

Not on its own. The activity specifies replay at ±200-µs skew, whereas the hypothesis is stated under ≤200-µs clock skew. Results from the specified replay could inform that hypothesis, but the activity does not say that every skew value within the bound is replayed or that the full conditional claim has been proved.
Could I treat an unknown verdict on a gap-injected trace as a missed violation in the completeness check?

That would mix the two conditions. For a gap-tainted window, the behavior being checked is that the outcome stays unknown rather than becoming a false violation. The violation-completeness check applies to the lossless traces. An unknown outcome in the presence of a relevant gap is not, by itself, a failure of the stated lossless completeness condition.
What if the monitor reports a violation for a gap-tainted window just because its watermark passed the window?

That is precisely the kind of behavior the gap-taint check is meant to catch. Under the hypothesis being evaluated, the gap-tainted window stays unknown. Passing the window with a watermark cannot, by itself, supply the missing evidence needed to justify a violation.
On a lossless trace, should the check look for a violation before the response window expires?

The stated check concerns detection after expiry. Before expiry, the required response may still occur within its bound, so the activity should not recast the hypothesis as requiring an early violation verdict. It also does not specify an exact permitted delay between expiry and detection.
Can I say the oracle comparison will demonstrate that every possible bounded-response violation is detected?

Not from this activity alone. The proposed replay checks violation completeness against an oracle on the specified 10,000 traces. Even if those checks succeed, that is not the same statement as a proof covering every possible trace. No replay outcome has been supplied yet.
Does this activity check the instrumentation budget or deadline preservation too?

No. Its stated checks are gap taint and violation completeness using gap-injected and lossless trace replay at ±200-µs skew. It does not report worst-case execution-time overhead or a response-time analysis of deadlines. Those timing guarantees cannot be inferred from this replay description.
How should I describe the activity without implying that we have already observed favorable results?

State it as a planned evaluation: replay 10,000 gap-injected and lossless traces at ±200-µs skew, and compare the monitor’s gap-taint handling and lossless bounded-response violation detection after expiry with an oracle. Leave the outcomes open until the comparisons have been made.
The replay results are in. Across 10,000 traces at ±200-µs skew, gap-tainted windows stayed unknown; in the lossless replay, the monitor detected 100% of bounded-response violations after expiry.

Those are the two observed outcomes of the replay. Gap-tainted windows retained an unknown verdict, rather than becoming violations because a watermark passed them. For the lossless traces, every bounded-response violation in the oracle comparison was detected after the applicable window expired. The 100% figure describes the violations in this replay, not every possible trace.
Can I say the gap result answers my concern about advancing watermarks past dropped sequence numbers?

It addresses that concern in the tested traces: gap-tainted windows stayed unknown despite the monitor’s progress. That means the reported replay did not turn those unknown outcomes into violation verdicts. The result does not, on its own, establish how every possible gap pattern would behave.
Does ‘stayed unknown’ tell us whether a response actually occurred in the missing telemetry?

No. It describes the monitor’s verdict for a window tainted by a gap. The result does not recover the dropped observation or establish what it contained. Unknown preserves that uncertainty instead of treating missing telemetry as proof that no response occurred.
How precisely should I state the 100% detection result?

In the lossless replay at ±200-µs skew, 100% of the bounded-response violations identified for comparison were detected after expiry. That keeps the denominator tied to violations in the replay and preserves the after-expiry condition. It does not imply that every window was a violation or specify the time elapsed between expiry and detection.
Did the result show immediate detection at the expiry instant?
It reports detection after expiry, not at the exact expiry instant. No numerical detection latency is given, so ‘immediate’ would add a claim the evidence does not state.
The hypothesis referred to clock skew of ≤200 µs. Can I now say the entire range was covered?

The reported replay was at ±200-µs skew. That is the condition to name for these observations. The result does not say that every skew value within ≤200 µs was tested, so it should not be described as coverage of the entire range.
What about the 10,000 traces—were there 10,000 lossless traces and another 10,000 gap-injected traces?

The result says ‘across 10,000 traces’ and reports outcomes for gap-tainted windows and lossless replay. It does not give a separate count for each category. Saying 10,000 for each would add an unsupported split.
Would it be fair to say this establishes sound verdicts under any telemetry loss?

That would be broader than the reported evidence. The observed gap-tainted windows stayed unknown across the stated replay, which avoids the false-violation concern for those windows. The result does not claim to cover every loss pattern or every kind of verdict.
Does the lossless result establish completeness for every possible bounded-response violation?

It establishes 100% detection among the bounded-response violations in the lossless replay, after expiry. It does not turn a finite replay of 10,000 traces into a universal proof. The observation is strong within its stated scope, but its scope remains the reported traces and skew setting.
Are these results also evidence that monitoring adds less than 5% worst-case execution time per control job?

No. This evidence concerns verdict behavior in trace replay: unknown outcomes for gap-tainted windows and 100% detection of lossless bounded-response violations after expiry. It provides no worst-case execution-time measurement or response-time analysis, so it does not establish the instrumentation budget or deadline preservation.
Please give me a concise results statement that keeps all those boundaries clear.

Across 10,000 replayed traces at ±200-µs skew, gap-tainted windows stayed unknown. In the lossless replay, 100% of bounded-response violations were detected after expiry. These are results for the reported replay; they do not specify detection latency, coverage of every skew value within ≤200 µs, or timing overhead and deadline outcomes.
I’m ready to adopt gap-tainted unknown verdicts and skew-aware watermarks. The reason is that the replay showed no false violations and complete lossless detection at ±200 µs.

That states the decision and its basis clearly. Gap-tainted outcomes will remain unknown rather than being declared violations from incomplete telemetry, and the monitor will use skew-aware watermarks. The supporting replay showed no false violations and complete detection of bounded-response violations in the lossless replay at ±200-µs skew. Those are replay findings, not a claim about every possible trace or skew setting.
What am I committing to by adopting gap-tainted unknown verdicts?

You are choosing to preserve an inconclusive verdict when a telemetry gap taints the bounded-response outcome. In that situation, the monitor must not treat the missing observation as proof that a required response was absent. ‘Unknown’ is a deliberate verdict policy for that uncertainty, not another name for a violation.
And does adopting skew-aware watermarks mean a watermark can never move past a gap?

No. The decision concerns what the monitor may conclude, not a blanket prohibition on watermark movement. Skew-aware watermarks can track progress while the verdict for a gap-tainted outcome remains unknown. Moving a watermark must not, by itself, erase the uncertainty that makes a violation verdict unjustified.
I want the two adopted elements to work together, not sound like unrelated features.

They work together in the verdict rule. Skew-aware watermarks help the monitor interpret progress despite timing uncertainty across cores. Gap-tainted unknown verdicts prevent that progress from being mistaken for complete evidence when telemetry is missing. The decision is to use both without letting watermark advancement convert an uncertain bounded-response outcome into a violation.
How should I describe the replay support without overstating it?

Say that the replay showed no false violations and complete lossless detection at ±200-µs skew. That reports the favorable behavior observed under the stated replay condition. It does not turn the observation into a universal guarantee for all traces, all loss patterns, or other skew settings.
Does ‘complete lossless detection’ mean we detect violations even when telemetry is lost?

No. ‘Lossless’ is an essential qualifier: the replay’s complete detection result concerns bounded-response violations when telemetry was not lost. For gap-tainted outcomes, the adopted verdict is unknown where the missing telemetry leaves the outcome unresolved. The two statements should not be merged into a promise of complete detection under loss.
Should I say the replay proved there can be no false violations?

The decision says the replay showed no false violations. ‘Proved there can be none’ would be stronger than that observation. You can cite the replay as support for adopting the policy while keeping the claim confined to what was observed.
Is ±200 µs the amount of time the monitor waits before deciding?
No. Here ±200 µs identifies the skew setting for the replay result. It is not a specified waiting period or a bounded-response deadline. The decision does not state a verdict-latency value.
Does this decision settle whether the runtime-verification design preserves the controllers’ deadlines?

No. This decision adopts a verdict policy and skew-aware watermarks on the stated replay evidence. The cited findings concern false violations and lossless detection at ±200 µs; they do not state a deadline-analysis result or a monitoring-overhead result.
Give me a final decision sentence that preserves both the choice and its reason.
Adopt gap-tainted unknown verdicts and skew-aware watermarks, supported by replay that showed no false violations and complete lossless detection of bounded-response violations at ±200-µs skew.
The next plan is to integrate the adopted gap-tainted monitors into the dual-core controller, then verify ≤5% per-job WCET overhead and all deadlines via response-time analysis.

That keeps integration and timing verification together without claiming either is complete. The plan is to put the adopted monitors in the dual-core controller, account for their effect on each control job’s worst-case execution time, and use response-time analysis to check that all specified deadlines remain satisfied.
What does ‘gap-tainted’ mean for the monitors we are integrating?

It identifies the adopted verdict behavior: when missing telemetry leaves a bounded-response window uncertain, its verdict remains unknown rather than becoming a violation on the basis of the gap. Integration should retain that behavior. The plan does not specify a new verdict rule for the controller.
Does the plan require a new monitor design for two cores?

It calls for integrating the adopted monitors into a dual-core controller. It does not describe a redesign or specify how monitor work is assigned between the two cores. The dual-core setting matters to the integration and timing checks, but the plan leaves those implementation details open.
Please clarify what the ≤5% figure applies to.

It is a limit on monitoring overhead in worst-case execution time for each control job. A controller-wide average below 5%, or an average across jobs, would not by itself verify the per-job requirement. The planned check needs to establish that each applicable job stays at or below the ≤5% WCET-overhead limit.
If the overhead check passes, can we assume the deadlines pass too?

No. The overhead bound and deadline preservation are distinct checks. A job could meet the ≤5% per-job WCET-overhead limit without that fact alone establishing that every specified deadline still holds. The plan therefore includes response-time analysis for the deadline check.
What role does the monitoring overhead play in response-time analysis?

The analysis must account for the execution-time cost of the integrated monitoring when assessing the controller’s response times. Otherwise, a deadline conclusion would not reflect the system the plan proposes to run. The node does not prescribe a particular WCET-assessment method or response-time formula.
